blocks.html: In Sources for Egyptian History you met the evidence Egyptians left themselves: inscriptions, papyri and monuments. For centuries after hieroglyphs fell silent, though, Europe knew Egypt almost only through a second kind of source: what Greek and Roman visitors wrote about it. Those accounts are still worth reading, as long as we read them the way a historian does.

Herodotus (5th century BC), Diodorus of Sicily (1st century BC) and Strabo (late 1st century BC) described Egypt from their own travels and from what priests, guides and older books told them. What they saw with their own eyes is often good; what they were told about the distant past is often hearsay.

A source is only as good as its access to the events. Herodotus could watch the Nile flood and Egyptian customs of his day, so those passages can be checked against other evidence and often hold up. But he wrote about two thousand years after the pyramids were built, could not read hieroglyphs, and depended on interpreters. For the pyramid age he was a tourist hearing stories, not a witness.

blocks.title: How far back was the pyramid age?
blocks.q: Khufu reigned c. 2589–2566 BC. Herodotus was in Egypt around 450 BC. About how long before his visit did Khufu begin his reign?
steps: Both dates are BC, so subtract: 2589 − 450 = 2139.
Round it, since Khufu's dates are uncertain by decades: about 2,100 years.
For comparison, about 2,475 years separate Herodotus from today. He stood almost as far from Khufu as we stand from him.
blocks.a: About 2,100 years.

blocks.title: Sorting an account
blocks.q: Herodotus says the Great Pyramid took twenty years to build and that 100,000 men worked on it in three-month shifts. How should a historian treat this?
steps: Ask how he knew. He was told this by guides about two thousand years after the building, and he could not read the inscriptions.

Ask what other evidence says. Archaeologists have excavated the workers' town and cemeteries beside the Giza plateau; most modern estimates of the workforce are much smaller, though the figures are still argued over.
Conclusion: a tradition worth recording, but not a measurement. It tells us what Egyptians of the 400s BC said about their past.
blocks.a: Treat it as a later tradition, checked against archaeology, not as an eyewitness count.

blocks.html: Treating Herodotus as an eyewitness to the pyramid age. He wrote about two thousand years after it, from what guides told him. A quick check: before trusting a classical statement about Egypt, ask whether the writer could have seen it himself. The Nile flood, yes; Khufu's workforce, no.

Manetho, an Egyptian priest who wrote in Greek in the 3rd century BC, could read the old records. His history survives only in quotations by later writers, but it gave us the numbered dynasties: see Manetho's Dynasties.

blocks.html: Writers like Herodotus and Strabo visited an Egypt where priests still carved hieroglyphs. That world ended slowly. Temples closed under Christian emperors, the last priests died, and by the 5th century AD no one alive could read the script. It stayed unreadable for about 1,400 years.

Once the last trained readers were gone, scholars assumed hieroglyphs were not writing for sounds at all but pure symbols, each picture standing for a sacred idea. That belief, from Horapollo in late antiquity to Athanasius Kircher in the 1600s, kept the script locked.

Hieroglyphs look like pictures, and some of them do stand for what they show. Late Greek writers knew that much and built a whole theory on it. But most signs in a real text stand for sounds. A reader who looks for a hidden meaning in every picture will invent a long mystical sentence where the Egyptian text says something plain, like a name and a title. The wrong theory made every attempt fail.

The Hieroglyphica, a Greek book under the name of Horapollo, probably dates from the 4th or 5th century AD. It explains nearly two hundred signs, each as an allegory. A few meanings are right, but the reasons given are not. The book says a goose means "son" because geese love their young. In fact the bird sign used in the word for "son" (a pintail duck) writes the consonants zꜣ, the same consonants as the word itself: a sound pun, not a lesson about birds. The manuscript was found on the Greek island of Andros in 1419 and printed in 1505, and Renaissance scholars took it as the key to Egypt.

blocks.html: Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit scholar in Rome, published huge volumes on Egypt, including Oedipus Aegyptiacus (1652–1655). His "translations" turned short inscriptions on obelisks into pages of mystical philosophy. Yet he made one lasting contribution: he studied Coptic, the language of Egypt's Christians, and argued that it descended from the ancient language. He also saw that the water sign could stand for the sound m, matching the Coptic word ⲙⲟⲟⲩ "water". That Coptic link would later prove vital.

blocks.title: How long was the script forgotten?
blocks.q: The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in AD 394. Champollion announced his decipherment in AD 1822. How many years lie between?
steps: Both dates are AD, so subtract: 1822 − 394.
blocks.a: 1,428 years, or "about 1,400 years".

blocks.title: Symbol or sound?
blocks.q: A scholar of the 1600s sees an owl in a cartouche and writes that it stands for "wisdom and the night". What is the modern reading, and why did he go wrong?
steps: The owl is the sound sign for m, one letter in a spelled-out name.
He assumed every picture was a symbol. That is the error behind Horapollo and Kircher: they never tested whether the signs could spell words.
A sound reading can be tested: the same signs must spell the same names wherever they appear. A symbolic reading cannot be tested at all.
blocks.a: The owl writes m; reading it as a symbol made the text unreadable.

blocks.html: Thinking hieroglyphs were always understood as sounds. For about 1,400 years European scholars thought they were mystical symbols. Remember the dates: last carved AD 394, read again in 1822.

blocks.html: Egypt never stopped being famous, even while no one could read its script. Some of the best publicity came from obelisks: tall, single stones with a pointed top, carved with the names of kings. Egyptian kings set them up in pairs before temples, especially at Heliopolis and Thebes, as signs of the sun god.

Roman emperors shipped Egyptian obelisks to Rome and Constantinople as trophies. In the 1800s three more went to Paris, London and New York. Rome now has eight ancient Egyptian obelisks, more than any other city, Egypt included.

An obelisk is a portable monument: one stone, already finished and inscribed. Moving it proved the power of whoever could do it. For Rome after conquering Egypt in 30 BC, and for European states in the 1800s, a re-erected obelisk was a statement of reach. The inscriptions on them, copied and argued over, kept scholars curious about the script.

blocks.title: Why "Cleopatra's Needles"?
blocks.q: The London and New York obelisks are nicknamed "Cleopatra's Needles". Were they made for Cleopatra?
steps: Their hieroglyphs name Thutmose III, who reigned c. 1479–1425 BC, with later lines added by Ramesses II.
The Romans moved them from Heliopolis to Alexandria about twenty years after Cleopatra VII died in 30 BC, to stand before a temple she had begun.
So the nickname comes from Alexandria, not from who made them. Thutmose III lived about 1,400 years before Cleopatra.
blocks.a: No: they were made for Thutmose III, and only later stood in Cleopatra's city.

blocks.title: Reading a date on an obelisk
blocks.q: An obelisk carries the cartouches of Ramesses II, but its oldest inscription names Seti I, his father. What does that tell you?
steps: Kings often added their own inscriptions to a monument begun by an earlier king.
The oldest name (Seti I) dates the start of the work; the later name (Ramesses II) shows when it was finished or claimed.
This is why the Flaminio obelisk is listed under both kings.
blocks.a: It was begun under Seti I and inscribed again under Ramesses II.

blocks.html: Thinking "Cleopatra's Needles" were made for Cleopatra. They were made for Thutmose III, more than a thousand years earlier. Check the cartouche, not the nickname.

blocks.html: By the late 1700s Europe had Horapollo's symbols, travellers' sketches and a few obelisks in Rome, but no accurate record of Egypt's monuments. That changed with a war.

In 1798 Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Egypt, then part of the Ottoman Empire, and brought about 167 scholars, engineers and artists. They measured and drew the monuments, and their results were published as the Description de l'Égypte, from 1809 into the 1820s. The book, and the Rosetta Stone found by the army in 1799, set off the modern study of Egypt.

Decipherment and archaeology both need accurate copies. Before 1798, European images of Egypt were often guesses. The French team worked like surveyors: they measured temples, made plans and sections, copied inscriptions and recorded plants, animals and daily life. A scholar in Paris or London could now study a temple at Edfu or Karnak without going there, and compare inscriptions side by side.

blocks.title: Who gets the credit?
blocks.q: Did Napoleon's soldiers decipher hieroglyphs?
steps: Soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in July 1799, and the scholars saw at once that its Greek text might unlock the other two.
But reading it took more than twenty years of work by others: Thomas Young from 1814, and Jean-François Champollion, who announced his system in 1822.
The expedition supplied the stone and accurate copies, not the reading.
blocks.a: No. They found the key; reading it took another two decades.

blocks.title: A soldier-artist's book
blocks.q: Vivant Denon, an artist on the expedition, published a best-selling account of his travels with drawings in 1802. Why might historians value the Description above it for studying temples?
steps: Denon sketched quickly while following the army up the Nile.
The Description was produced by teams who measured buildings and drew plans to scale, over several years.
For details like the layout of a temple, a measured plan is better evidence than a quick sketch, though both record monuments that have since been damaged.
blocks.a: Because its plans and copies were measured, not sketched.

blocks.html: Crediting Napoleon's soldiers with deciphering hieroglyphs. They found the Rosetta Stone in 1799; reading it took until 1822. Keep the two dates apart.
The expedition was a military invasion, and it ended in defeat. The scholarship it produced and the damage of the war are both part of the story.

blocks.html: In July 1799, during Napoleon's expedition, French soldiers rebuilding a fort near the town of Rosetta (Rashid) in the western Delta found a broken slab of dark granodiorite covered in writing. Their officer, Pierre-François Bouchard, saw that it held three blocks of text, one of them in Greek, and reported it at once.

The Rosetta Stone carries one decree, issued by a council of priests at Memphis in 196 BC in honor of King Ptolemy V, written three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic and in Greek. That makes two languages, Egyptian and Greek, in three scripts. Taken by the British in 1801, it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

Scholars could read the Greek. If the other two blocks said the same thing, the Greek was a translation that could be matched against them, word by word and name by name. A text in a known language next to one in an unknown script is the most useful thing a decipherer can have: it supplies the meaning, so the work becomes finding which signs carry which words.

blocks.html: The stone is about 112 cm tall, 76 cm wide and 28 cm thick, and weighs about 760 kg. It is only part of a taller stela. Copies of the same decree were set up in temples across Egypt; the text itself says so. The decree praises the young king, lists the benefits he gave the temples, and orders that his statue and the decree be placed in every temple, written in "sacred, native and Greek letters".

blocks.title: Two languages or three?
blocks.q: A guidebook says "the Rosetta Stone is written in three languages". Correct it.
steps: Hieroglyphic and Demotic are two scripts for one language, Egyptian. Hieroglyphs were the formal script; Demotic was the everyday cursive of the time.
The third text is in Greek, the language of the Ptolemaic government.
So: three scripts, two languages.
blocks.a: "Two languages (Egyptian and Greek) in three scripts."

blocks.html: Saying the stone has three languages. There are two, Egyptian and Greek, in three scripts. Check by asking of each text: what language would a speaker of the time recognize? The top two are both Egyptian.
You can find the Rosetta Stone on the site Timeline, beside the other events of the decipherment.

The Rosetta Stone reached London in 1802. Copies of its texts went to scholars all over Europe. One of the first to make real progress was the English physician and physicist Thomas Young (1773–1829), already famous for showing that light behaves as a wave.

From 1814 Young studied the stone and showed three things: the ovals called cartouches hold royal names; the cartouche that appears where the Greek names Ptolemy holds that name, so some of its signs must stand for sounds; and Demotic is related to hieroglyphs and mixes sound signs with word signs. He published his results in the article "Egypt" in the Encyclopaedia Britannica (1819).

Names are the decipherer's best friend. A name like Ptolemaios has to be spelled out by sound, whatever the script, because a foreign name has no picture. If the Greek text mentions Ptolemy at a certain point, and the hieroglyphic text has a framed group at the matching point, that group is probably the name, and its signs should spell p, t, o, l, m, y and s.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: Ptolemy's cartouche, sign by sign: p, t, o, l, m, y, s. Young worked out several of these values; Champollion confirmed them all.

blocks.html: Young's method was comparison. He lined up the texts, counted how often words recurred, and found about 80 matches between hieroglyphic and Demotic groups. Working from royal names such as Ptolemy's, he proposed sound values for 13 signs. By a modern count, six were right, three partly right and four wrong. He also thought sound spelling was used only for foreign names like Ptolemy, while native Egyptian words were written with symbols. That last idea held him back.

blocks.title: Finding the name
blocks.q: The Greek text names Ptolemy several times. How could Young find the hieroglyphic word for Ptolemy without reading any hieroglyphs?
steps: Look for a group of signs that repeats in the hieroglyphic text about as often as Ptolemy's name repeats in the Greek.
Notice that one repeated group is inside an oval frame, the cartouche, and royal names are what an Egyptian decree would honor.
Check the position: the group appears where, by the order of the Greek, the name should be.
blocks.a: By matching a repeated, framed group to the repeated name in the Greek.

blocks.title: Sounds in a foreign name
blocks.q: If the cartouche spells Ptolemaios, which sound should its first sign carry, and how can that be tested?
steps: The Greek name begins with p, so the first sign, the stool, should be p.
Test it on another name that contains p, such as Cleopatra: the same stool sign should appear in the position of p.
A value that works in two different names is unlikely to be a coincidence.
blocks.a: p, tested by finding the same sign in another name with p.

blocks.html: Giving all the credit to one man. Young made real progress: cartouches, the Ptolemy reading, the nature of Demotic. Champollion built the full system and showed that native Egyptian words used sound signs too. Both belong in the story.

Young also worked hard on Demotic: his Rudiments of an Egyptian Dictionary in the Ancient Enchorial Character was published in 1831, after his death. Some historians call him the decipherer of Demotic.

blocks.html: Jean-François Champollion (1790–1832) had studied languages since boyhood, Coptic most of all. He read Young's work and went further. In 1822 he showed that the same sound signs spelled the names of Greek and Roman rulers in many inscriptions, and then that they also spelled the names of native pharaohs who had lived long before any Greek came to Egypt.

Champollion compared the cartouches of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, found the signs they shared, and built a list of sound signs. Reading copies of cartouches from Abu Simbel, he found the same signs in native names: Ramesses and Thutmose. On 27 September 1822 he read his Lettre à M. Dacier to the Academy in Paris, setting out the sound signs of Greek and Roman names.

Two names that share sounds should share signs. Ptolemaios and Kleopatra both contain p, o and l, so if both cartouches are sound spellings, the signs for p, o and l should appear in both, in the right positions. They do. The test also turned up a surprise: Ptolemy writes t with a loaf, Cleopatra with a hand. Champollion concluded that a sound could have more than one sign, which is true.

blocks.html: Copies of temple inscriptions from Abu Simbel showed a cartouche with a sun disk, then an unknown sign, then two signs that he knew as s from Ptolemy. In Coptic the word for "sun" is ⲣⲏ (rē), and the unknown sign looked like the one in a word the Greek text glossed as "birth", Coptic ⲙⲓⲥⲉ (mise). Ra-mes-s: Ramesses, a native king. A second cartouche began with the ibis of the god Thoth: Thoth-mes, Thutmose. Champollion's later accounts date this to September 1822; some historians think the full reading came months later. Either way, sound signs were not just for foreigners.

blocks.title: Which sign is p?
blocks.q: Ptolemy's name has p first; Cleopatra's has p fifth. Which sign must be p?
steps: Find the sign that is first in Ptolemy.
Check the fifth sign in Cleopatra. Both are the reed stool.
The stool is p in both places, so the value is confirmed.
blocks.a: The stool.

blocks.title: A native name
blocks.q: The cartouche shows the ibis of Thoth, then the ms sign, then s. Why does this reading matter more than Ptolemy?
steps: Thoth is an Egyptian god, and the name means "Thoth is born". This king, Thutmose, was a pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty, more than a thousand years before the Ptolemies.
So sound signs were part of the Egyptian system from long before Greek rule, not a trick for foreign names.
That meant every inscription, of every period, could now be read.
blocks.a: It shows that sound signs spelled native Egyptian names, so the whole script was readable.

blocks.html: You have seen Champollion's breakthrough step by step. Stand back and ask what made it possible. Many people had tried before him, some for centuries. What did the successful approach have that the others lacked?

Three keys opened the script: a bilingual text (the Rosetta Stone and others) that gave the meaning; royal names, which had to be spelled by sound and could be matched across scripts; and Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian, which gave the sounds and the words behind the signs.

Each key solves a different part of the puzzle. A translation tells you what a text says but not how its signs work. Names tell you the sounds of some signs, but only in names. Coptic tells you what Egyptian words sounded like, so when sound signs spell out a group like m-s, you can recognize it as a real word, ⲙⲓⲥⲉ "give birth". Without all three, the decipherment would have stalled.

blocks.title: Why not the Greek alone?
blocks.q: The Greek text of the Rosetta Stone tells us exactly what the decree says. Why wasn't that enough to read the hieroglyphs?
steps: A translation gives meaning, not sounds. Knowing a passage means "the king gave silver to the temples" does not tell you which signs spell "silver".
The hieroglyphic text is also damaged, and the two versions do not follow each other word for word.
Names and Coptic were needed to link signs to sounds, and sounds to words.
blocks.a: Because a translation does not show which signs carry which sounds and words.

blocks.title: Using Coptic
blocks.q: Sound signs in a cartouche spell r-ꜥ-m-s-s, with the sun sign first. How does Coptic help confirm that the first part means "sun" and the middle "born"?
steps: Coptic, written in Greek letters with vowels, has ⲣⲏ "sun" and ⲙⲓⲥⲉ "to give birth".
Those words have the same consonants as the sign groups: r for the sun, m-s for birth.
So the reading is not a guess: it matches real Egyptian words that were still known through the Coptic Church.
blocks.a: The Coptic words for "sun" and "give birth" have the same consonants.

blocks.html: Thinking the Greek translation alone was enough. Without Coptic, the sounds of the words would have stayed unknown. A quick check: could you read a page of a language you have never heard, given only a loose translation? You would know what it means, but not how to read it.
Champollion also overestimated how close Coptic was to the language of the pharaohs, and some of his readings were wrong for that reason. Coptic is a guide, not a key that fits every lock.

blocks.html: Once names and Coptic had opened the door, Champollion turned to whole texts. In his Précis du système hiéroglyphique (1824) he described the script as, in his words, "figurative, symbolic and phonetic" all at once, in the same text and often in the same word.

Hieroglyphs are a mixed system. Sound signs stand for one, two or three consonants. Word signs (logograms) stand for a whole word, often what they picture. Determinatives, written at the end of a word, are not read aloud but show what kind of thing the word means.

A mixed system solves real problems. Egyptian writing shows consonants, not vowels, so many words would look alike. A word sign makes a common word quick to write, and a determinative tells words with the same consonants apart. That is also why the symbolic theory was half right: some signs do mean what they show. Its mistake was to think that all of them did. The same sign can even play different roles in different words: the sun disk is a word sign in rꜥ "sun", but a determinative in words for time and light.

blocks.title: Reading the roles in a word
blocks.q: The word for "sky" is written with a stool, a loaf, and a picture of the sky. Which signs are read aloud?
steps: The stool is p and the loaf is t: both sound signs.
The sky picture ends the word. It is a determinative: it shows the meaning, sky, and is not pronounced.
So the word is read pt.
blocks.a: Only the stool and the loaf (p and t).

blocks.title: A word sign with helpers
blocks.q: In ꜥnḫ "life", the ankh sign stands for all three consonants ꜥ, n and ḫ, yet it is followed by the signs for n and ḫ. Why?
steps: The ankh sign is a three-consonant sign: ꜥnḫ.
The extra n and ḫ repeat sounds the ankh already holds. They are phonetic complements: reading aids, not new sounds.
So the word is still read ꜥnḫ, not ꜥnḫnḫ.
blocks.a: They are phonetic complements that confirm the reading.

blocks.html: Thinking hieroglyphs are an alphabet once decoded. The 24 one-consonant signs work like an alphabet, but most words also use two- and three-consonant signs, word signs and determinatives. If you read every sign aloud, a determinative will give you a sound that is not there.
The grammar of the signs is taught in full in Three Kinds of Signs and Determinatives.

sources.name: Alan Gardiner, Egyptian Grammar (1927; 3rd ed. 1957), the chapters on the writing: sound signs, word signs and determinatives

blocks.html: Champollion died in 1832, aged 41, ten years after his first results. His system was not accepted by everyone. Some scholars, such as Gustav Seyffarth, attacked it for the rest of their lives. Two things settled the argument: better grammar, and new bilingual texts.

Richard Lepsius (1810–1884) corrected the system: in a published letter to Ippolito Rosellini (1837) he showed that many signs stand for two or three consonants, not one, and explained phonetic complements. The Canopus Decree, a decree of 238 BC in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, found by Lepsius at Tanis in 1866, then let scholars check readings against a new, well-preserved text.

A decipherment is proved when it predicts. If the readings are right, a newly found text in the old script should come out, when read by the rules, saying what its Greek version says. The Canopus Decree was found decades after the system was published, so no one could have tuned the rules to fit it. When its hieroglyphs, read by Champollion's and Lepsius's rules, matched its Greek, the decipherment was proved beyond reasonable doubt.

blocks.title: Correcting a single-consonant reading
blocks.q: Champollion read the sign in the middle of Ramesses' name as m. Lepsius showed it is ms. Why does the name still come out as Ramesses?
steps: Champollion read sun + m + s + s: Ra-m-s-s.
Lepsius: the sun (rꜥ), then ms, then s and s. The first s repeats the s of ms as a phonetic complement; the second writes sw "him": rꜥ-ms-sw, "Ra is the one who bore him".
Both readings give the same consonants here, which is why the error hid. In other words it mattered: a sign that holds two consonants cannot be read as one.
blocks.a: The extra s is still there; the correction shows up in other words.

blocks.title: Why a new find is the test
blocks.q: Why was a text found in 1866 better proof than the Rosetta Stone itself?
steps: The rules were worked out from the Rosetta Stone and other known texts, so they fit those texts by design.
A text found later is an independent test.
The Canopus Decree read correctly by the old rules, so the rules were right, not just fitted.
blocks.a: Because no one could have shaped the rules to fit it.

blocks.html: Thinking the decipherment was accepted at once. It was argued over until new texts proved it. Keep the dates in mind: 1822 announced, 1837 corrected, 1866 confirmed.

blocks.html: The Description de l'Égypte made Egypt fashionable. In the decades that followed, European consuls in Egypt competed to collect statues, coffins and papyri for the museums and private collections of their home countries. Muhammad Ali, Egypt's ruler, gave them permits to dig; local workers did the labor.

In the early 1800s, collectors such as Giovanni Belzoni, working for the British consul Henry Salt, and Bernardino Drovetti, the French consul, shipped thousands of objects to Europe. Many are now treasures of the British Museum, the Louvre and the Egyptian Museum in Turin. But almost nothing was recorded about where or how they were found, so much of what those objects could have told us is lost.

An object's findspot is evidence. A statue from a temple sanctuary means something different from the same statue in a later house or a rubbish pit. Collectors wanted the object, not the information around it, and they dug fast, broke through walls and sometimes used force. Once a site is dug carelessly, the arrangement of things in it is gone for good.

Belzoni (1778–1823), a tall Paduan who had performed as a strongman in London, came to Egypt in 1815 to sell a water-lifting machine. Hired by Salt, he moved the colossal head of Ramesses II known as the "Younger Memnon" from the Ramesseum to the river in 1816; it is now in the British Museum. In 1817 he cleared the sand from the entrance of the great temple at Abu Simbel and found the tomb of Seti I in the Valley of the Kings, the finest decorated tomb then known. He also found the entrance to Khafre's pyramid at Giza.

blocks.title: What was lost?
blocks.q: A painted coffin reached a European collection in 1820 with a label saying only "from Thebes". What information is missing, and why does it matter?
steps: We do not know which tomb it came from, who was buried with it, or what lay beside it.
Without the tomb, we cannot date it by its surroundings, link it to a family, or tell whether it was reused.
The coffin is still beautiful, but as historical evidence it has lost most of its story.
blocks.a: Its findspot and associations; without them it can be studied only as an object.

blocks.title: Belzoni's credit and cost
blocks.q: Belzoni is praised for his finds and blamed for his methods. Give one reason for each.
steps: Praise: he found Seti I's tomb and opened Abu Simbel, and he drew and described what he saw; some of his records are still useful.
Blame: he dug for objects to ship, damaged structures to move them (he broke column bases at the Ramesseum to clear a path), and kept no systematic record of context.
Both are true: judge him by the standards of his time, and learn from what was lost.
blocks.a: Great discoveries; no method for recording context.

blocks.html: Thinking early collectors were archaeologists. They took objects, often with no record of where they came from. Check any museum object's history: if its findspot is unknown, ask why.
In 1835 Muhammad Ali issued a decree against exporting antiquities and planned a museum in Cairo. It was poorly enforced, but it was a start: see Laws on Antiquities.

By the 1850s the collectors had stripped many sites. The change began with a young Frenchman sent to Egypt by the Louvre in 1850 to buy Coptic manuscripts. Auguste Mariette (1821–1881) spent the money digging instead.

Mariette found the Serapeum at Saqqara, the underground burial galleries of the Apis bulls, in 1850–1851. In 1858 the ruler Said Pasha made him head of a new Antiquities Service, with control over excavation in Egypt, and in 1863 he opened a national museum at Bulaq in Cairo, so that finds could stay in Egypt.

Protection needs an institution. A law means little without people to enforce it, a register of what exists, and a place to keep finds. Mariette's Service licensed excavators, took charge of sites and sent important finds to the museum, where they were catalogued. It was far from perfect, but it put control of Egypt's antiquities inside Egypt.

blocks.title: Why a museum in Egypt mattered
blocks.q: Before 1863, a statue dug up in Egypt usually ended up in Europe. How did the Bulaq museum change that?
steps: Licensed excavators now had to report finds to the Service.
Important finds went to the museum in Cairo, where they were registered and displayed.
Egypt now had a place to keep its own past, and a reason for visitors to come to Cairo to see it.
blocks.a: It gave finds a home in Egypt and a register.

blocks.title: A mixed record
blocks.q: Mariette is called a founder of Egyptian archaeology. Name one strength and one weakness of his work.
steps: Strength: he built the Service and the museum, cleared great sites such as the Serapeum, and was among the first in Egypt to photograph finds.
Weakness: he dug quickly with large workforces, recorded little by later standards, lost many notes in an 1878 flood, and kept Egyptians, such as the young Ahmed Kamal, out of senior posts.
A fair verdict holds both.
blocks.a: He built institutions; his digging and his treatment of Egyptian colleagues fell short.

blocks.html: Thinking all early finds left Egypt. From 1858 Mariette's Service began the effort to keep them, and from 1863 the museum gave them a home. Many objects still left, under a system that divided finds with foreign excavators, but the direction had changed.
The Antiquities Service was run by French directors until 1952. Its successor today is the Supreme Council of Antiquities. Egyptian scholars' place in it is told in Egyptian Egyptologists.

After Mariette, the next great change in method came from an Englishman with almost no schooling and a gift for measurement. William Matthew Flinders Petrie (1853–1942) first went to Egypt in 1880 to survey the Giza pyramids, to test a popular claim that the Great Pyramid encoded a sacred unit of length. His measurements showed the claim was false.

From the 1880s Petrie excavated with a new kind of care. He recorded small finds and broken pottery, not just statues; he noted where each thing was found; he kept his workers paid for finds so that objects were reported, not sold; and he published his results quickly, often within a year.

Most of what a site holds is ordinary: potsherds, beads, tools, bones. Those are also the things that change most often with fashion, so they date a site. A dig that keeps only the statues throws away the clock. Petrie's approach was to note and compare the smallest details, because that is where change shows.

blocks.title: Why pay for a bead?
blocks.q: Petrie paid his workers a small reward for every object they found, even a bead. Why was that a good method?
steps: Without a reward, a worker who found a small object could sell it to a dealer, and it would vanish from the record.
With a reward, it was handed in and its findspot recorded.
It made small finds worth reporting, which is what a dated record needs.
blocks.a: It kept finds, and their findspots, in the record.

blocks.title: Publishing as part of the dig
blocks.q: Why did Petrie insist on publishing each season's work quickly?
steps: Excavation removes the evidence it studies. After a dig, the published record is all that remains.
An unpublished dig is, for everyone else, a destroyed site with nothing to show.
Quick publication let other scholars use and check his results.
blocks.a: Because the publication is the site, once it has been dug.

blocks.html: Thinking only gold and statues matter. Petrie showed that broken pots can date a site, as the next topic, Seriation (Sequence Dating), shows. Ask of any find: what does it tell us, not what is it worth?
Petrie's views on race, common in his time, are now rejected, and some of his work reflected them. His field methods are what lasted.

sources.name: W. M. Flinders Petrie, The Pyramids and Temples of Gizeh (1883); Methods and Aims in Archaeology (1904)

blocks.html: At Naqada and Diospolis Parva (Hu), Petrie dug thousands of graves of the Predynastic cultures, from before writing and before the kings. Nothing in them was dated. How could he put them in order?

Seriation puts things in order by their changing styles. Petrie listed the pottery types in each grave and arranged the graves so that each type appeared in one unbroken run. He numbered the result as sequence dates (SD 30, 31, … 80). They give an order, earlier and later, but not years.

Styles come in, are popular for a while, and fade out. A pot type made for fifty years will appear in graves from those fifty years, not scattered across centuries. So if graves are in the right order, each type's graves should sit together. The order that keeps every type together is most likely the order of time. Which end is earlier has to come from somewhere else: Petrie used a jar whose wavy handles shrank, over time, into a painted wavy line.

blocks.title: Finding the order
blocks.q: Using the table above, put the graves in a sequence in which every pot type appears in one unbroken run.
steps: Grave 4 has only A, and grave 1 has A and B, so 4 and 1 sit together: 4, 1.
Grave 3 has B and C, so it follows 1 (which shares B): 4, 1, 3.
Grave 2 has C and D, so it follows 3 (which shares C): 4, 1, 3, 2.
Check: A runs 4–1, B runs 1–3, C runs 3–2, D is only in 2. Every run is unbroken.
blocks.a: 4, 1, 3, 2 (or the reverse, 2, 3, 1, 4).

blocks.title: Which way is time?
blocks.q: Grave 4 contains jars with real wavy handles; grave 2 contains jars with only a painted wavy line. Which end of the sequence is earlier?
steps: Petrie found that the handles came first and shrank over time into a decoration.
So the grave with real handles, 4, is at the early end.
The sequence, earliest first, is 4, 1, 3, 2.
blocks.a: Grave 4 is earliest.

blocks.cap: Sequence dating ordered the graves of the Predynastic Period long before radiocarbon could give them years.

blocks.html: Taking sequence dates as years. SD 40 is earlier than SD 60, but the gap is not 20 years, or any number. Petrie started at 30 to leave room for earlier cultures not yet found. Absolute dates came later, from radiocarbon.

Petrie published the method in 1899 and used it in Diospolis Parva (1901). It was one of the first uses of seriation anywhere, and the same idea, grouping things by shared features, is used today with statistics and computers.

sources.name: W. M. Flinders Petrie, "Sequences in Prehistoric Remains," Journal of the Anthropological Institute 29 (1899); Diospolis Parva (1901)

blocks.html: Seriation orders separate graves. On a town site, archaeologists have something better: layers. Petrie noted the depth of his finds; his successors learned to read layers as a record of time.

Soil, rubbish, collapsed walls and windblown sand pile up over time. In an undisturbed sequence, lower layers are older than the layers above them (the law of superposition). Recording which layer every find came from lets archaeologists date finds by their context, and date layers by their finds.

A layer can only be laid down on top of something that is already there. So whatever lies beneath it formed first. A find in a layer gives a "no earlier than" date: a layer containing a seal of Ramesses II cannot have formed before his reign, although it could have formed long after. Archaeologists call that date the terminus post quem, "the limit after which".

blocks.title: Reading the section
blocks.q: In the section above, which is older: layer 3 or layer 2? What is the earliest that layer 2 could have formed?
steps: Layer 2 lies on layer 3, so layer 3 is older.
Layer 2 contains a seal naming Ramesses II, so it formed during or after his reign, which began c. 1279 BC.
It could have formed later than that, but not earlier.

blocks.title: A pit that breaks the rule
blocks.q: Layer 4 is a pit with a Roman coin, cut from the floor of layer 3 down into layer 5. It sits lower than layer 3. Is it older?
steps: No. A pit is dug down from a surface, so it is younger than every layer it cuts through.
The coin shows the pit was filled in Roman times or later, more than a thousand years after the house floor.
This is why excavators record the edges of pits, burrows and foundations: they mix the order.
blocks.a: No: the pit is the youngest feature in the section, apart from what lies above where it was dug.

By the 1910s, most people thought the Valley of the Kings had given up all its tombs. Howard Carter, who had trained as a young man with Petrie at Amarna, disagreed. He knew of objects naming Tutankhamun, a short-reigned king of the 18th Dynasty whose tomb had never been found.

On 4 November 1922 Carter's workers found a step cut in the rock under ancient workmen's huts. With his sponsor, Lord Carnarvon, he looked inside on 26 November. The tomb, numbered KV62, was nearly intact: about 5,400 objects. Carter and his team spent about ten years recording and clearing it; the last objects went to Cairo in 1932.

KV62 was the first royal tomb of the New Kingdom found with most of its contents in place, so every object's position mattered. Carter did not rush it. Each object got a number; Harry Burton photographed it where it lay; each was described on a record card and drawn; the chemist Alfred Lucas and the conservator Arthur Mace treated fragile pieces before they were moved. That record, now kept at the Griffith Institute in Oxford, is what scholars still use.

blocks.title: Why so slow?
blocks.q: The antechamber alone held hundreds of objects piled together. Why did clearing it take about two months, and the whole tomb about ten years?
steps: Each object had to be numbered, photographed in place and drawn before it was touched.
Many were fragile: wood had shrunk, beads had lost their threads, textiles were brittle. They had to be stabilized first.
Moving one object without a record would destroy the evidence of where it lay. Slowness was the method.
blocks.a: Because recording and conserving each object came before moving it.

blocks.title: Weighing a "curse" story
blocks.q: Newspapers in 1923 linked Carnarvon's death to a pharaoh's curse. How would a historian test that idea?
steps: Check the cause: Carnarvon died of an infection, a known risk at the time, in a man already in poor health.
Check the others: Carter, who spent the most time in the tomb, lived until 1939; a 2002 medical study found no shorter lives among those present at the openings.
Check the source: no curse text was found in the tomb. The story started in newspapers competing for news, since one paper had exclusive access to the dig.
blocks.a: The evidence does not support it: a newspaper story, not a finding.

blocks.html: Believing in a curse. Carter and most of the team lived for years; the "curse" was a newspaper story. Check the dates: Carter died in 1939, sixteen years after the opening.

Unlike most earlier finds, almost all of the tomb's contents went to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo; a few small pieces that went astray have been returned over the years. Today the collection is shown together at the Grand Egyptian Museum at Giza.

blocks.html: Every topic in this unit has turned on one idea. Layers date finds; finds date layers; collectors who ignored both lost the story. This topic states the idea plainly.

An object's value as evidence depends on its context: where it lay, what it lay with, and which layer or feature held it. Excavation destroys the context it uncovers, so the record made during the dig (notes, plans, photographs, finds registers) is all that will remain of the site.

You can only dig a layer once. When it is removed, the arrangement of things in it is gone. A record lets later scholars ask new questions of a site no one can see again. That is why careful excavators dig slowly, record more than they think they need, and often leave part of a site untouched for future methods.

items: Findspot: where exactly the object was (site, area, depth, coordinates).
Association: what else was with it (the same grave, room or layer).
Layer or feature: which deposit held it, and how that deposit formed.
Condition: how it lay: in place, fallen, thrown away, reburied.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Amarna, Akhenaten's city, was lived in for only about twenty years, so its houses and workshops give unusually clear contexts. Tap a site.

blocks.title: Same object, two stories
blocks.q: Two identical scarabs: one was excavated in a child's grave at Amarna, beside the body's neck; the other was bought from a dealer. What can each tell us?
steps: The excavated scarab is dated by its grave and the city's short life; its place by the neck suggests it was worn as an amulet; it tells us about a child's burial.
The bought scarab can tell us its style and inscription, nothing more. It may even be a modern copy.
Same object, very different evidence.
blocks.a: The excavated one carries date, use and setting; the bought one only its own surface.

blocks.title: A famous context
blocks.q: The painted bust of Nefertiti was found in 1912 at Amarna in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose, among unfinished heads and plaster studies. How does that context change how we read the bust?
steps: A sculptor's workshop is where models were made and kept.
The bust has only one inlaid eye, and it lay among studies, so it was probably a workshop model rather than a finished statue for a temple or tomb.
The findspot, not the bust alone, tells us this.
blocks.a: It suggests the bust was a sculptor's model.

blocks.html: Valuing objects without their findspots. An object without context has lost most of its story. When you read about a find, look for where exactly it was found and what was with it.
You have met two ways of putting finds in order: seriation and stratigraphy. Both say "earlier" or "later" but never "how long ago". Archaeologists keep these two kinds of date strictly apart.

A relative date places something in order: older or younger than something else, or in the same phase. An absolute date places it in years on a calendar, with a margin of error: "c. 2500 BC", "AD 394", "1550 ± 30 BC".

The two answer different questions and have different weaknesses. A relative date can be certain without any calendar: a layer sealed under a floor must be older than the floor. An absolute date gives a number but always with an uncertainty, and that uncertainty matters. Mixing them up leads to false precision, such as treating Petrie's sequence date SD 40 as a year.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: Classify: (a) "Layer 3 formed after layer 4." (b) "The coffin dates to c. 1000 BC." (c) "The amulet is in the same style as amulets from the late 18th Dynasty."
steps: (a) An order without a year: relative.
(b) A year on the calendar with "c.": absolute.
(c) A style match places it in a phase. The 18th Dynasty has a dated span, so it is absolute in the end, but only as good as the dates of that style.

blocks.title: Combining both
blocks.q: A layer lies directly over a floor that contains a jar dated by radiocarbon to c. 1800 BC. What can you say about the layer?
steps: The floor is under the layer, so the layer is younger (relative).
The jar on the floor dates the floor to about 1800 BC (absolute).
So the layer formed after about 1800 BC: a relative order hung on an absolute date.
blocks.a: The layer is later than c. 1800 BC.

blocks.html: Mixing the two. "Earlier than the pottery in layer 3" is relative; "c. 2500 BC" is absolute. Ask: does this statement contain a year? If not, it is relative.

Egyptian history is mostly dated by the king lists and regnal years (see Dating by Regnal Years), then checked against astronomy and radiocarbon. The next topics take the scientific methods one by one.

blocks.html: In Radiocarbon and Egyptian Dates you saw how radiocarbon checks the historical chronology. Here is how the method works, step by step, and what it can and cannot date.

Living plants take in carbon from the air, including a tiny, steady share of radioactive carbon-14; animals get it by eating plants. After death no new carbon-14 comes in, and what is there decays at a fixed rate: half of it is gone after about 5,730 years (the half-life). Measuring how much is left gives the time since death, which must then be calibrated into calendar years.

Radioactive decay does not care about temperature, pressure or chemistry, so the clock runs at the same rate everywhere. After one half-life, half the carbon-14 is left; after two, a quarter; after three, an eighth. The fraction left therefore tells the age. Calibration is needed because the amount of carbon-14 in the air has varied over time; tree rings of known age, counted year by year, show how much, and a calibration curve (today IntCal20) converts a radiocarbon age to calendar years.

blocks.title: Counting half-lives
blocks.q: A piece of charcoal has 1/4 of the carbon-14 that living wood has. About how old is it?
steps: 1/4 = 1/2 × 1/2, so two half-lives have passed.
That is far older than dynastic Egypt: it would come from a site of the last Ice Age, before farming.
blocks.a: About 11,460 years.

blocks.title: A sample from the pyramid age
blocks.q: Reed from a mortar joint in an Old Kingdom pyramid is about 4,550 years old. What fraction of its carbon-14 remains? (Use fraction left = (1/2)^(age ÷ 5,730).)
steps: So a little less than 3/5 of the carbon-14 remains: less than one half-life has passed.

items: Yes: wood and charcoal, seeds and grain, reed, papyrus, linen, basketry, bone, hair, leather: anything once alive.
No: stone, metal or the clay of a pot (though food residue or straw inside a pot may be datable).
Care: wood can be much older than the building it was used in (a beam reused, or the inner rings of an old tree). Short-lived plants, like seeds and reeds, are best.

blocks.html: The first test of the method, by Willard Libby and James Arnold in 1949, used wood from the tombs of Djoser and Sneferu, whose age was known from history. In 2010 a team led by Christopher Bronk Ramsey dated 211 short-lived plant samples from museum collections, tied to particular reigns; the results agreed well with the standard historical chronology and placed the start of the New Kingdom in the range c. 1570–1544 BC.

blocks.html: Dating stone with radiocarbon. It dates once-living things: reeds, wood, seeds, linen. To date a stone building, date the organic material in it: reeds in mortar, wood in the roof, charcoal from the builders' fires.

blocks.html: Radiocarbon dates things that were alive. Pottery, the commonest find on any Egyptian site, was never alive. Luminescence dating can date it directly.

Crystals in clay and sediment, such as quartz and feldspar, slowly store energy from natural radiation in the ground. Heating to about 500 °C empties that store, and so does sunlight for some kinds of signal. Thermoluminescence (TL) dates the last time pottery was fired (or a flint was burned); optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dates the last time sediment saw daylight.

After the clock is reset, energy builds up again at a steady rate set by the radiation around the object. In the laboratory the sample is heated (TL) or lit (OSL), and the stored energy comes out as a faint glow. Measuring the glow gives the total dose absorbed since the reset; measuring the radioactivity of the sample and its surroundings gives the dose per year. Age = total dose ÷ dose per year.

blocks.title: Computing an age
blocks.q: A potsherd has absorbed 12 grays (Gy) of radiation since it was fired. The dose rate in its sample and soil is 3 Gy per thousand years. How old is it?
steps: Age = total dose ÷ dose rate.
12 Gy ÷ 3 Gy per thousand years = 4 thousand years.
So the pot was fired about 4,000 years ago, c. 2000 BC.
blocks.a: About 4,000 years.

blocks.title: Reading the margin
blocks.q: The lab reports the same sherd as 4,000 ± 8%. What range of years does that give?
steps: So about 3,700 to 4,300 years ago: too wide to choose between the late Old Kingdom and the Middle Kingdom. Pottery style would date it more closely.
blocks.a: About 3,680 to 4,320 years ago.

blocks.html: Expecting luminescence to be as precise as radiocarbon. Its margins are usually wider, often several centuries for Egyptian material. It is most useful where nothing else can be dated, and for testing whether a "pottery antiquity" was fired recently: forgeries fail a TL test.

Egypt is unusual: much of its archaeology can be dated by its own writing. As you saw in Dating by Regnal Years, Egyptians dated documents by the years of the reigning king. Combined with the king list, a date in a text becomes a date on our calendar.

An inscription with a king's name dates an object to that reign or later; one with a regnal year ("year 9 of Ptolemy V") dates it to a single year of the reign. Style, of pottery, coffins, statues or handwriting, dates objects to a period even without words. Each method has limits: names could be added later, carved over, or copied.

A date in a text is only as good as two links: the link between the text and the object, and the link between the reign and our calendar. A jar sealing names the king who reigned when it was sealed, so it dates the sealing. After 664 BC the reigns are fixed to the year; before that, our dates for them carry the margins of the chronology. And a statue carved for one king could be taken over by a later one who cut his own name into it.

blocks.text: From regnal year to calendar year

blocks.html: If a king's first regnal year is year X BC, his year n is about X − (n − 1) BC. Year 1 is the accession year, so subtract n − 1, not n. Egyptian regnal years did not start on 1 January, so the result can be one year off.

blocks.title: Year 9 of Ptolemy V
blocks.q: The Rosetta decree is dated to year 9 of Ptolemy V. His reign is counted from 204 BC. What year is that?
steps: Year 1 is 204 BC, so year 9 is 8 years later.
BC years count down: 204 − 8 = 196.
That matches the decree's date, 196 BC.

blocks.title: A name is not a date
blocks.q: A statue of Ramesses II bears his cartouche, but its face and style look like the reign of Amenhotep III, a century earlier. What happened?
steps: Ramesses II often took over the statues of earlier kings and recut their names (Egyptologists call this usurpation).
The style dates the carving; the cartouche dates the takeover.
So the statue was made under Amenhotep III and re-inscribed under Ramesses II.
blocks.a: An older statue re-inscribed: the style dates the making, the name the reuse.

blocks.html: Taking a king's name on an object as proof of its date. Names could be added later, or copied: heirlooms carry the names of earlier kings into later tombs, and later kings recut older statues. Check the style and the context too.

blocks.html: Excavation needs records because digging destroys. Inscriptions need records for a different reason: they are slowly destroyed anyway, by salt, groundwater, wind, tourism and old damage. Epigraphy is the careful copying and publishing of inscriptions and reliefs so that the record outlasts the wall.

An epigrapher copies an inscription exactly as it is: every sign, every crack, every damaged patch, without "improving" it. The Epigraphic Survey of the University of Chicago, founded by James Henry Breasted in 1924 and based at Chicago House in Luxor, has spent a century recording temples such as Medinet Habu this way.

A copy is used by people who will never see the wall, perhaps after the wall is gone. If the copyist fills a gap with what he expects, the reader cannot tell the guess from the evidence. If he leaves out a faint sign, the reader cannot recover it. So the rule is: draw what is there, mark what is damaged, and put restorations only in the edition, clearly marked.

items: A large photograph is taken of a section of wall and enlarged.
At the wall, an artist traces the carving onto the print in pencil, checking against the stone.
The lines are inked; then the photograph is bleached away, leaving a drawing on white paper.
Two Egyptologists, working separately, check the drawing against the wall sign by sign (this is collation) and mark corrections.
The artist makes the corrections, and the drawing gets a final check at the wall before publication.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: Every sign of ḥtp-dj-nsw, "an offering that the king gives". An epigrapher records each sign as carved, including the direction the signs face.

blocks.title: Why not just photograph it?
blocks.q: Cameras are cheap and exact. Why does the Epigraphic Survey still draw?
steps: A photograph records everything at once: carving, stains, salt crust, old paint, cracks and shadows. On a damaged wall these can hide signs or look like signs.
A trained epigrapher, looking at the stone in different lights, can tell a chisel cut from a crack.
The drawing records the epigrapher's judgment, checked by two others; the photograph is kept beside it as evidence.
blocks.a: Because light, stains and damage hide details that a trained eye, checked by collation, can recover.

blocks.title: Recording damage
blocks.q: Half of a sign has flaked off a wall. What should the copy show?
steps: The surviving half, exactly as it is.
The edge of the damaged area, drawn as damage (often by hatching).
Not the missing half. If the sign can be identified, the edition can say so, marked as partly preserved.
blocks.a: What survives, and where the damage is; nothing invented.

blocks.html: Thinking a photograph is enough. Light and damage hide details that careful copying recovers. Look at any photo of a weathered wall and ask: is that a sign, or a crack?

Since the 1990s the Survey has also cleaned and conserved monuments, and its volumes are free to download. Rising groundwater, which brings salt into the stone, is one of the main threats it records against.

blocks.html: The Chicago method is one way of making a faithful copy, or facsimile. Others have been used for two centuries, and new ones arrive every decade. Each has a job it does best.

Recording methods range from hand tracing on clear film laid on the wall, through measured drawing on photographs, to photogrammetry (a 3-D model computed from many overlapping photographs), laser scanning (millions of measured points), and reflectance transformation imaging (RTI: photographs lit from many directions). None replaces the trained eye that checks the result.

Each method captures different evidence. Tracing records what the copyist sees, at full size, but touching the wall can harm fragile paint. Photogrammetry and laser scanning record shape and depth, so they show weathered relief that a flat photo misses. RTI lets a viewer move the light afterwards, so shallow carving appears in raking light. But a computer cannot know whether a groove is a chisel mark or a crack; an epigrapher must decide.

steps: Every visitor brings heat, humidity and dust into a tomb, which damage its paintings.
A facsimile made from high-resolution recording lets people see the tomb's decoration without harming it.
The recording itself also preserves the tomb's present state for study.
blocks.a: To protect the real tomb while letting people see it.

blocks.html: Thinking new technology replaces the expert. Every method still needs a trained eye to check it. A scan records a groove; only an epigrapher can say whether it is a sign.

blocks.html: An epigrapher's copy shows the wall as it is. An edition goes one step further: it gives the text in transliteration or translation, with the editor's restorations, and it uses brackets to show the reader exactly what is on the stone and what the editor supplied.

Editions mark text that is lost but restored by the editor with square brackets [ ]; signs that are damaged but still partly visible with half brackets ⸢ ⸣; and words the ancient scribe left out, supplied by the editor, with angle brackets ⟨ ⟩. Curly braces { } mark signs the scribe wrote by mistake, which the editor would delete.

Restoring a text is often possible, because Egyptian inscriptions repeat set formulas. The offering formula, for example, is so regular that a missing "Osiris" or "bread and beer" can be supplied with confidence. But a confident guess is still a guess. Brackets let a reader see at once how much of a sentence is evidence and how much is reconstruction, and decide how far to trust an argument built on it.

blocks.html: These marks come from the conventions agreed by classical scholars at Leiden in 1931, which editors of Greek, Latin and Egyptian texts adapted. Details vary between editions, so check the key at the front of any edition you use.

blocks.title: Reading an edited line
blocks.q: An edition reads: "an offering that the king gives [to Anubis], ⸢he who is upon⸣ his mountain, that he may give ⟨bread and⟩ beer". What is certain on the stone?
steps: "to Anubis" is in square brackets: it is lost and restored.
"he who is upon" is in half brackets: damaged, but traces are visible.
"bread and" is in angle brackets: the scribe never carved it; the editor added it.
Fully certain: "an offering that the king gives", "his mountain", "that he may give" and "beer".
blocks.a: Only the unbracketed words are fully on the stone.

blocks.title: Building on a restoration
blocks.q: A scholar argues that this stela was set up for Anubis's cult. The name "Anubis" appears only in square brackets. How strong is the argument?
steps: Square brackets mean the name is restored, not seen.
The restoration may be good (Anubis often follows "the king gives" in this formula), but Osiris is just as common.
An argument resting only on a restoration is weak until other evidence supports it.
blocks.a: Weak: it rests on a restoration.

blocks.html: Reading restored words as certain. Brackets show what the editor supplied. When you quote an edition, keep its brackets.

From Mariette's museum at Bulaq to the newest buildings in Giza, Egypt has kept a growing share of its past at home. But two centuries of collecting, buying and division of finds have spread Egyptian objects around the world.

The largest collections are in Cairo and Giza: the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir Square (opened 1902), the Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids (fully opened in November 2025) and the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization, home of the royal mummies since 2021. Abroad, the great collections include the British Museum in London, the Louvre in Paris, the Neues Museum in Berlin, the Egyptian Museum in Turin and the Metropolitan Museum in New York.

Where an object is today depends on how it left the ground. Objects found by the collectors of the early 1800s usually went to Europe. Under the system of dividing finds that lasted into the 20th century, foreign excavators often took home a share. Objects found since Egypt's modern laws stay in Egypt. So the map of collections is a map of the history of archaeology itself.

steps: The stone was taken by the French army and handed to the British under the terms of the French surrender in 1801.
Tutankhamun's tomb was found under a later system: almost all of its contents went to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
The date and circumstances of discovery decide where an object went.

blocks.html: Thinking every important object is in Egypt. Many of the most famous are abroad, like the Rosetta Stone in London and the bust of Nefertiti in Berlin. When you hear of a famous object, ask where it is and how it got there.

blocks.html: Some of the best-known objects in museums abroad left Egypt when Egypt was under Ottoman, British or French influence. Egypt has asked for some of them back. Museums holding them have mostly said no. This is a real debate, argued in good faith on both sides; this topic sets out the arguments, not a verdict.

Those who favor return argue that objects taken in colonial times left without fair consent, belong to Egypt's national heritage, and can now be cared for and seen in Egypt's own museums. Those who favor keeping them argue that they were acquired legally under the laws and agreements of the time, have been well kept and studied, and are seen by huge international audiences, and that museums are often barred by law from giving them up. Each case turns on how the object was acquired, the laws of the time, and what is best for the object and the public.

The debate is hard because the two sides often agree on the facts and disagree on what matters most. A division of finds signed by both parties in 1913 can be legal and still look unfair a century later. A museum in London can serve millions of visitors and still hold an object that many Egyptians see as part of their own story. Reasonable people weigh legality, history, access and care differently.

That supports keeping the bust.

blocks.q: In 2019 the Metropolitan Museum returned the gilded coffin of Nedjemankh to Egypt, two years after buying it. Why was there no debate in that case?
steps: Investigators showed that the coffin was looted in 2011 and sold with a forged export license.
It was stolen property under the laws in force when it left Egypt, so neither law nor ethics supported keeping it.
The debate over return concerns objects that left legally, or under disputed terms, long ago, not recent thefts.
blocks.a: It was recently stolen, so its case was settled by law, not argued.

blocks.html: Expecting one obviously right answer. Each case turns on how an object was acquired, the laws of the time, and what is best for the object and the public. Before taking a side on any case, find out how that object left Egypt.
Middle paths are also proposed: long-term loans, shared research and exhibitions, replicas and digital access, and returns of objects whose removal was clearly illegal.
The return debate often turns on law: what the law said when an object left Egypt. Here are the main laws, Egyptian and international, and when they apply.

Egypt's Law 117 of 1983 on the protection of antiquities makes antiquities public property, bans trade in them, and forbids private possession except for holdings registered under the law. Internationally, the 1970 UNESCO Convention commits the states that join it to prevent the illicit import, export and transfer of cultural property. Egypt joined in 1973.

A law usually applies from the day it takes effect, not before. So the same kind of object can be legal or illegal depending on when it left: a statue exported with a permit in 1920 is not stolen under Law 117, while one smuggled out in 2011 is. That is why museums today ask for an object's history ("provenance") back to 1970 or earlier: that date has become the main test of whether an object entered the market legally.

blocks.title: Before or after?
blocks.q: A coffin left Egypt with a valid export permit in 1925. Another was dug up illegally and smuggled out in 2012. How do the laws apply?
steps: In 1925 export with a permit was legal, and neither Law 117 nor the 1970 Convention existed. The first coffin is not stolen property, whatever one thinks of the system.

Same kind of object, different law: the date of export decides.

blocks.title: Foreign courts
blocks.q: In 2002 a New York antiquities dealer was convicted in a U.S. court of dealing in objects smuggled out of Egypt. Why did Egypt's Law 117 matter in an American court?
steps: U.S. law forbids dealing in stolen property.
The court accepted that Law 117 makes Egypt the owner of antiquities found after 1983, so objects taken without permission were stolen.
A country's ownership law can therefore protect its antiquities abroad.
blocks.a: It made the objects Egypt's property, so dealing in them was dealing in stolen goods.

blocks.html: Thinking old finds and new finds are treated the same. Laws apply differently to objects that left before and after them. Always ask: when did this object leave Egypt, and what was the law then?

blocks.html: Because excavation destroys what it uncovers, modern archaeologists try to learn as much as possible before, or instead of, digging. That work is called survey.

Archaeologists find and map sites by field survey (walking the ground and recording what lies on the surface), aerial and satellite images, and geophysics (instruments that sense buried walls and pits). Much can be learned without a shovel, and digging can then be aimed where it will answer a question.

Buried things change the ground above them. A mud-brick wall holds water differently from the sand around it, so crops grow differently over it and it shows as a line in an air photograph. Burnt material and fired brick have a different magnetism from the soil, so a magnetometer picks them up. Hard foundations reflect radar waves. Each method measures a contrast, and a contrast in the right shape is a wall, a street or a pit.

Comparing them with recent images shows what has been lost, and where looting has happened.

blocks.html: Thinking archaeology always means digging. Much is learned without a shovel. Survey finds sites, maps them and shows where a small excavation would answer a question, so that less of the site has to be destroyed.
After 2011, repeated satellite images were used to map looting pits at many Egyptian sites, a sad but useful example of what survey from space can show.
Some of the newest evidence about ancient Egypt comes from laboratories, not trenches. Survey sees under the ground; lab science sees inside objects and bodies, often without harming them.

CT scanning looks inside mummies without unwrapping them, showing age, health, injuries and how the body was prepared. Ancient DNA, residue analysis (what was in a pot) and isotope studies (what people ate and where they grew up) are newer; their results are exciting but often small in scale and still debated.

A new method is only as good as its checks. CT scans are images that many doctors can read and compare, so their basic results are rarely in doubt. Ancient DNA, by contrast, is fragile and easily contaminated by modern DNA, and a study may rest on a few individuals from one site. A careful reader asks: how many samples, from where, and has another team confirmed it?

blocks.html: South of Aswan lies Nubia, a long, narrow strip of temples, forts and villages along the Nile. In the 1950s Egypt decided to build a new high dam at Aswan, and its lake would flood Nubia for hundreds of kilometers. The answer was the largest survey and rescue effort archaeology had ever attempted.

When the Aswan High Dam was built (1960–1970), UNESCO led an international campaign (1960–1980) to record and save Nubia's monuments. Teams from many countries surveyed and excavated the threatened land, and engineers moved 22 monuments, including the temples of Abu Simbel and Philae, to higher ground. Many sites, and whole Nubian villages, were lost under Lake Nasser.

A dam lake is permanent. Anything not recorded or moved before the water rose would be lost for good, so the campaign had to work at a speed no excavation normally allows. That is why it combined rapid survey of the whole valley, quick excavation of the most important sites, and the cutting and moving of temples too important to lose.

blocks.html: Histories of Egyptology often read like a list of Europeans: Mariette, Petrie, Carter. But Egyptians worked on every excavation, and Egyptian scholars have led the study of their own past for more than a century, often against the resistance of the foreign officials who ran the Antiquities Service.

Egyptian scholars such as Ahmed Kamal (died 1923), the first Egyptian Egyptologist, and Selim Hassan (1886–1961), who excavated at Giza from 1929 to 1939, built Egyptology in Egypt. Today Egyptian archaeologists lead much of the excavation and conservation in the country.

Who does the research shapes what is asked. Egyptian scholars wrote in Arabic for Egyptian readers, connected the ancient language with Egyptian Arabic and Coptic, and argued that Egypt's past belonged first to Egyptians. Their careers were long held back: the Antiquities Service had only French directors until 1952, and some, like Mariette, kept Egyptians out of senior posts.

blocks.q: A guidebook says "Khufu's boat was found in 1954." Who found it, and who rebuilt it?
steps: Kamal el-Mallakh, an Egyptian archaeologist, found the sealed pit beside the Great Pyramid in 1954.
Ahmed Youssef Moustafa, chief restorer of the Antiquities Department, spent years rebuilding the boat from 1,224 pieces.
It is now shown at the Grand Egyptian Museum.
blocks.a: Kamal el-Mallakh found it; Ahmed Youssef Moustafa rebuilt it.

blocks.title: The workers behind the finds
blocks.q: Petrie trained a group of workmen from the town of Quft, whose families dug on expeditions for generations. Why does that matter for the history of Egyptology?
steps: Skilled Egyptian foremen and workers did much of the actual excavation, and their knowledge passed down in families.
Their names rarely appear in the books, though their skill shaped the results.
A full history includes the people who did the digging.
blocks.a: Because Egyptians did much of the work that Europeans published.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptology is only a European field. Egyptians have been central to it for over a century, as scholars, curators, excavators and skilled workers. When you read about a discovery, look for the Egyptian names.

The decipherment, as you have seen, began with hieroglyphs carved in stone. But carving is slow. For everyday writing Egyptians used a quicker hand, written with a reed brush and ink. Greek writers later called it hieratic, "priestly", because in their day priests used it for religious books.

Hieratic is the cursive form of the hieroglyphs: the same signs, with the same sound values and the same language, simplified and joined for fast writing in ink. It appears at the very beginning of Egyptian writing, in the late Predynastic (Naqada III) period, and was used alongside hieroglyphs for more than three thousand years.

When you write quickly with a brush, you drop detail. An owl becomes a few strokes; a seated man becomes a hook. Signs that often stand together run into each other (ligatures). That is all hieratic is: hieroglyphs written fast. Because each hieratic sign still corresponds to a hieroglyph, a reader can convert one into the other, sign by sign.

blocks.title: Which came first?
blocks.q: A student writes: "Hieroglyphs came first; hieratic was invented later as a shortcut." What does the evidence say?
steps: Ink inscriptions in a cursive hand appear on pottery and labels from the very start of writing, at the end of the Predynastic Period.
Carved hieroglyphs and written hieratic developed side by side, each suited to its material.
So hieratic is not a later invention; it is the brush form of the same script from the start.
blocks.a: They were used side by side from the beginning.

blocks.title: One script, two looks
blocks.q: Why can an Egyptologist who knows hieroglyphs learn to read hieratic, but not instantly?
steps: The signs, values and language are the same, so everything known about reading hieroglyphs still applies.
But the shapes are simplified, joined and different from scribe to scribe and century to century.
A reader must learn the hieratic form of each sign, usually from a table of sign forms by date (a palaeography).
blocks.a: Same system; new shapes to learn.

blocks.html: Thinking hieratic came after hieroglyphs. The two were used side by side from the beginning. What came later, in the 7th century BC, was Demotic, which grew out of hieratic.
A later, very cursive form used at Thebes for legal documents and letters, called abnormal hieratic, was replaced by Demotic in the 26th Dynasty.

blocks.html: If you imagine Egyptian writing as carved temple walls, you see only a small part of it. Hieratic, in ink, was the working script of Egypt: the script of offices, homes, schools and libraries.

Letters, accounts, legal records, lists of workers, mathematics, medicine, literature and religious books were all written in hieratic, on papyrus, on wooden boards and on ostraca, potsherds and flakes of limestone used as cheap notepaper.

Papyrus was valuable and stone carving was slow, so everyday writing went on whatever was at hand. A potsherd costs nothing; a scribe could jot a laundry list, a receipt or a school exercise on it. Most of what survives is from dry places: desert cemeteries, and villages like Deir el-Medina, where the workmen who cut the royal tombs left thousands of ostraca.

blocks.title: Why ostraca?
blocks.q: Why did a workman at Deir el-Medina write a receipt on a flake of limestone instead of papyrus?
steps: Papyrus had to be made from reeds and was valuable.
Limestone flakes were everywhere around the tombs the workmen were cutting.
For a short note, a free flake did the job: an ostracon.
blocks.a: Because it was free and at hand; papyrus was costly.

blocks.title: Telling text types apart
blocks.q: A hieratic papyrus lists numbered problems, each followed by steps and an answer. What kind of text is it, and which famous example is like it?
steps: Numbered problems with worked steps are a teaching text in mathematics.
The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, copied c. 1550 BC, is the best-known example.
blocks.a: A mathematical text, like the Rhind Papyrus.

blocks.html: Thinking most Egyptian writing was carved. Most of it was written in ink, in hieratic. Carvings survive well and are easy to see; papyri and ostraca survive mostly in dry places, so even what we have is a fraction.

Since hieratic has no standard font and every scribe's hand differs, Egyptologists do not usually print it. Instead they transcribe it: they write out each hieratic sign as the hieroglyph it stands for. Then they read the hieroglyphs as they would any inscription.

Reading hieratic takes three steps: transcribe each hieratic sign into its hieroglyph (using a table of sign forms by date, such as Georg Möller's), transliterate the hieroglyphs into the Egyptological alphabet, and translate. Editions often print the hieroglyphic transcription beside a photograph of the papyrus.

Transcription separates two jobs. The first, identifying each cursive sign, needs a specialist's eye and a palaeography table, and it is where most uncertainty lies, so it is shown openly in the edition. The second, reading the hieroglyphs, is the same as for any carved text. A reader who doubts a transcription can check the photograph, sign by sign.

A Middle Kingdom literary papyrus and a Ramesside account can look very different, so palaeography tables arrange each sign's forms by date and by manuscript. Experienced readers learn to date a papyrus roughly from its handwriting alone, much as a historian can tell an 18th-century letter from a modern one.

blocks.html: Languages change. The Middle Egyptian of the Middle Kingdom was the classical language. By the reign of Tutankhamun and the later New Kingdom, everyday speech had moved on, and scribes began to write the way people talked. Egyptologists call this stage Late Egyptian (about 1350–700 BC).

Late Egyptian has articles: pꜣ "the" before masculine nouns, tꜣ before feminine nouns and nꜣ (followed by n) before plurals, and wꜥ "a". It builds new verb forms with helper verbs, much as English says "I did go" or "I am going". Middle Egyptian stayed in use beside it for formal inscriptions.

In Middle Egyptian, pꜣ, tꜣ and nꜣ were demonstratives, "this" and "these". Words like that often weaken into articles as a language changes, as Latin ille "that" became Italian il "the". Late Egyptian shows the same path. Spelling also changed: weak consonants such as ꜣ, w and the feminine t were often left out, because they were no longer pronounced.

blocks.title: Two languages in one reign
blocks.q: Ramesses II's temple walls are mostly in Middle Egyptian, while letters from his reign are in Late Egyptian. Why?
steps: Middle Egyptian had become the formal, traditional language, like Latin in medieval Europe.
Monuments meant for eternity used the classical language; everyday letters used the language people spoke.
So the choice depended on the kind of text, not only the date.
blocks.a: Formal monuments kept the classical language; everyday writing used Late Egyptian.

blocks.html: Late Egyptian is mostly written in hieratic, on papyrus and ostraca, so it is read through hieroglyphic transcription. Its spelling can look strange to a reader of Middle Egyptian: scribes mixed old spellings with new sounds, and added or dropped signs freely. Out of Late Egyptian grew the next stage of the language, Demotic, from about 700 BC.
Thinking Middle Egyptian vanished in the New Kingdom. It stayed in use for formal texts beside Late Egyptian, and was still carved in temples under the Ptolemies and Romans.

blocks.html: Late Egyptian was the language of the New Kingdom's offices and homes, and also of some of its liveliest literature. Most of these texts are written in hieratic, on papyrus and ostraca, and are read through hieroglyphic transcription.
Late Egyptian texts include letters, legal and official records such as the tomb-robbery papyri, stories such as the Report of Wenamun and the Tale of Two Brothers, and love poems.

Language follows use. Middle Egyptian stayed for monuments, so the texts closest to daily life are the ones written in the spoken language: a letter to a son, a court record of thieves' confessions, a story told for pleasure. That is why Late Egyptian texts often sound more like real speech, with dialogue, jokes and complaints.
