blocks.title: Story or report?
blocks.q: Wenamun was once read as a real travel report. Why do most Egyptologists today read it as literature, based on real conditions?
steps: It is told with dialogue, irony and a well-shaped plot.
Its people and places are sometimes vague in ways an official report would not be.
It still shows real conditions of its time: Egypt's weakened standing abroad at the end of the New Kingdom. Scholars debate how much of it happened.
blocks.a: Its literary craft; but it reflects real conditions, and the question is still debated.

blocks.title: Evidence from a court
blocks.q: What can the tomb-robbery papyri tell a historian that a temple wall cannot?
steps: They record what witnesses and thieves actually said, under questioning, about real tombs.
They show officials' rivalries, the workings of justice and the hard times at the end of the 20th Dynasty.
A temple wall shows the king's ideal; these show daily reality.
blocks.a: Daily reality: crime, courts and officials at work.

Hieratic was already a fast hand. In the 7th century BC, scribes in the north of Egypt developed an even faster one. Herodotus called it the "popular" script, dēmotika, and we still call it Demotic. The Egyptians called it "document writing".

Demotic grew out of northern hieratic in the 7th century BC and spread across Egypt under the 26th Dynasty. It is very cursive: many signs are joined into groups that stand for whole words or endings. It is written right to left, in ink. It was used until the 5th century AD.

Each step of cursive writing loses more of the picture. In Demotic, a group that once was several hieroglyphs may be written as one quick stroke pattern, learned as a whole. That makes Demotic fast to write, and hard to read for anyone who knows only hieroglyphs. Its signs still descend from hieroglyphs through hieratic, so specialists can trace most groups back to their origins.

blocks.title: Which text is Demotic?
blocks.q: On the Rosetta Stone, which text is the Demotic, and what language is it in?
steps: The stone has hieroglyphs at the top, Demotic in the middle and Greek at the bottom.
Demotic is an Egyptian script, so the middle text is in Egyptian, the language of the people, in its everyday hand.
blocks.a: The middle text; it is Egyptian.

blocks.title: Why Demotic was read before hieroglyphs
blocks.q: Scholars read names in the Demotic of the Rosetta Stone in 1802, twenty years before the hieroglyphs were read. Why was it easier at first?
steps: Its text is better preserved: 32 lines, against 14 broken lines of hieroglyphs.
Names in it could be matched letter by letter with the Greek, and some Demotic groups looked like an alphabet.
But scholars then wrongly thought Demotic was purely alphabetic; it also has word signs, like hieroglyphs.
blocks.a: Better preserved and easier to match with the Greek names.

blocks.html: Confusing Demotic with Greek on the Rosetta Stone. Demotic is the middle text, an Egyptian script. The Greek is at the bottom.

Because Demotic began as "document writing", the largest group of Demotic texts is business: contracts, receipts, accounts, letters and petitions. But Demotic also has a rich literature, written when the hieroglyphic temples were still active under the Ptolemies and Romans.

Demotic was used for contracts (sales, leases, marriage settlements), letters, tax receipts on ostraca, legal codes, religious and magical texts, and stories, like the tales of Setne Khamwas, and wisdom books, like the Instruction of Ankhsheshonq.

A script used every day by thousands of scribes leaves a huge record. Demotic documents survive by the tens of thousands, many from towns in the Faiyum and Middle Egypt, where dry rubbish heaps preserved papyrus. They let historians follow real families through several generations: who married whom, who owned which field, who paid which tax.

blocks.title: Why a story uses an old prince
blocks.q: The hero of the Setne tales, written down in Ptolemaic and Roman times, is based on Khaemwaset, a son of Ramesses II who lived about a thousand years earlier. Why use him?
steps: Khaemwaset was remembered as a scholar who restored old monuments: a natural hero for a story about ancient books and magic.
Setting a story in a famous past gave it weight, as tales of King Arthur do in English.
The tales tell us how Egyptians of the later periods saw their own past.
blocks.a: He was remembered as a scholar of the ancient past.

blocks.title: Reading a family's life
blocks.q: A historian has a family's Demotic marriage contract, two land leases and ten tax receipts. What can she learn that a temple inscription could not tell her?
steps: Who married whom, and what property the wife brought or was promised.
Which fields the family farmed, and what they paid.
The real economy of ordinary people, not the ideals shown on temple walls.
blocks.a: The everyday economic and family life of ordinary people.

blocks.html: Thinking Demotic was only for business. It also has a rich literature: adventure tales, wisdom books, myths and religious texts.
You have met the Rosetta Stone and the Demotic script. They meet in the middle of the stone: the 32 lines of Demotic between the broken hieroglyphs and the Greek.

The Demotic text of the Rosetta Stone has 32 lines and is the best preserved of its two Egyptian texts. It was the first to yield results: Silvestre de Sacy and Johan Åkerblad read its personal names in 1802, and Thomas Young built his work on comparing it with the Greek and with the hieroglyphs.

A decipherer needs as much text as possible. The hieroglyphic section is broken: only the last 14 lines survive, and many of those are damaged at the ends. The Demotic is nearly complete, so names and phrases could be found in it where the hieroglyphs are missing. Comparing Demotic groups with the hieroglyphs above also showed that the two scripts were related.

blocks.title: Åkerblad's names
blocks.q: In 1802 Åkerblad found every personal name of the Greek text in the Demotic. How could he do that without reading Demotic?
steps: He knew where in the Greek each name came, and how often.
He looked for groups in the Demotic at matching places that repeated as often, and compared their shapes with each other.
Then he tested sound values from one name on another, and used Coptic to guess at words like "Greek" and "temple".
blocks.a: By matching positions and repetitions with the Greek, then testing the sounds.

blocks.title: Young's comparisons
blocks.q: Thomas Young found about 80 groups in the Demotic that matched groups in the hieroglyphs. What did that show?
steps: If Demotic groups correspond to hieroglyphic groups, the two scripts are related.
So Demotic is not an alphabet invented separately: it descends from hieroglyphs and uses word signs as well as sound signs.
This corrected Åkerblad, who had thought Demotic was alphabetic.
blocks.a: That Demotic is derived from hieroglyphs and mixes kinds of sign.

blocks.html: The decree itself names its three scripts: it orders that it be written in "sacred", "native" and "Greek" letters, that is, hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek. Scholars still debate which version was drafted first.
Thinking the hieroglyphic part is the longest. It is the most damaged: only 14 lines survive. The Demotic has 32 and the Greek 54.

blocks.html: By the Roman period, Egyptian was written in Demotic, a script so cursive that few outside the temple schools could read it. Greek letters, meanwhile, were everywhere: Greek was the language of government since the Ptolemies, and many Egyptians could read it. As Christianity spread in Egypt, Egyptian Christians began to write their own language in the Greek alphabet.

Coptic is the last stage of the Egyptian language, written from about the 3rd century AD, chiefly by Egyptian Christians, in the Greek alphabet plus six or seven letters taken from Demotic for sounds Greek lacked. It is the same language as the hieroglyphs, three thousand years later.

An alphabet with vowels is easier to learn than thousands of signs, and the Christian scriptures were to be read by ordinary believers. Greek letters were already familiar, so scribes used them, and borrowed Demotic signs where Greek had no letter for an Egyptian sound, such as sh (ϣ) or f (ϥ). Earlier experiments, now called Old Coptic, wrote Egyptian words in Greek letters from about the 1st century AD, mostly in magical texts; standard Coptic took shape in the 3rd and 4th centuries.

blocks.title: One language or two?
blocks.q: A student says Coptic is "a different language that replaced Egyptian". Correct it.
steps: Coptic words descend from earlier Egyptian words: rmṯ "person" became ⲣⲱⲙⲉ.
Its grammar continues Late Egyptian and Demotic grammar.
What changed was the script, and the sounds over time, not the language family.
blocks.a: Coptic is Egyptian, in its last stage, written in a new alphabet.

blocks.title: Why Christians?
blocks.q: Why is Coptic mostly the writing of Egypt's Christians?
steps: The old scripts were tied to the temples and their priests, who wrote hieroglyphs and Demotic.
Christian communities wanted scripture, prayers and letters that ordinary people could read, in their own language.
Monasteries copied and wrote in Coptic for centuries; the Nag Hammadi codices, buried in the 4th century and found in 1945, are Coptic books.
blocks.a: Because Christians needed an easy script for scripture in their own language.

blocks.html: Thinking Coptic is a separate language from ancient Egyptian. It is Egyptian, written in a new alphabet. That is why Champollion, who knew Coptic, could recognize the words that hieroglyphs spelled.
Coptic took many words from Greek, especially for religion, law and trade: by one estimate up to two fifths of the vocabulary of literary Coptic.

Coptic writes Egyptian in a version of the Greek alphabet. Most letters are the 24 letters of Greek, in their rounded book forms, in Greek order, from alpha to omega. Here is how they are read in Coptic.

Coptic uses all 24 Greek letters, from ⲁ (alpha) to ⲱ (ō), for Egyptian sounds, and adds letters from Demotic for sounds Greek lacked. Some Greek letters, such as ⲅ, ⲇ, ⲍ and ⲝ, appear mostly in words borrowed from Greek.

Greek had letters for sounds Egyptian did not use, like d and g; Egyptian had sounds Greek did not write, like sh and f. So the Greek letters for d and g stay mainly in Greek loanwords, while native words need the borrowed Demotic letters. The vowels are the great gain: Greek letters write a, e, ē, i, o, ō and u, which hieroglyphs never showed.

blocks.html: Coptic letters also served as numbers, marked with a line above, as in Greek: ⲁ 1, ⲃ 2, … ⲓ 10, ⲕ 20, … ⲣ 100, ⲥ 200, and so on to ⲱ 800. So ⲣⲕⲉ is 100 + 20 + 5 = 125.
Coptic manuscripts usually write all letters in the same rounded book hand, without separate small letters; the small and capital forms shown above are a modern printing convention.

Reading Coptic with Greek sounds for every letter. Some letters are mostly used in Greek loanwords, and a few have their own Coptic values, like ⲟⲩ for ou. Learn the Coptic values, not the Greek ones.
The 24 Greek letters could not write every Egyptian sound. Coptic scribes filled the gaps with letters taken from the Demotic script, each one a simplified sign that had once been a hieroglyph.

Sahidic Coptic adds six letters from Demotic: ϣ (sh), ϥ (f), ϩ (h), ϫ (a sound like the ch of "church"), ϭ (ky) and ϯ (ti). Bohairic, the northern dialect, adds a seventh, ϧ (kh, as in Scottish "loch").

Greek had no letters for sh, f or a plain h, and these sounds are common in Egyptian. Rather than invent new shapes, scribes took the Demotic signs that already wrote them. You can still see the line of descent: the Coptic letter for f comes, through Demotic, from the horned viper hieroglyph, which wrote f.

blocks.html: Hieroglyphs, hieratic and Demotic write consonants only. That is why Egyptologists add e between consonants to say words aloud: nfr is said "nefer" by convention. Coptic, with its full set of vowel letters, is the first stage of the language to show how words actually sounded.

Because Coptic writes vowels, it shows how Egyptian words sounded late in their history: rn "name" is ⲣⲁⲛ, ran; nfr "good" is ⲛⲟⲩϥⲉ, noufe. But Coptic shows the sounds of the first millennium AD, not the sounds of the pyramid age.

Every spoken language changes, and three thousand years is a long time: compare the English of today with that of a thousand years ago. Some Egyptian consonants disappeared (the r at the end of nṯr "god" is gone in ⲛⲟⲩⲧⲉ, noute), some changed (the ḫ of ḫpr became the sh of ϣⲱⲡⲉ), and the vowels moved. So Coptic is excellent evidence for late Egyptian sound, and only indirect evidence for earlier sound.

blocks.title: Hearing a word
blocks.q: How was ꜥnḫ "life" pronounced in Coptic times? Its Coptic form is ⲱⲛϩ.
steps: ⲱ = ō, ⲛ = n, ϩ = h.
So: ōnh. The ꜥ left no trace, and ḫ became h.
The familiar "ankh" is a modern convention, not the Coptic sound.
blocks.a: ōnh.

blocks.title: Earlier evidence
blocks.q: Can Coptic tell us exactly how Khufu's builders said nfr?
steps: No. Coptic ⲛⲟⲩϥⲉ shows the word about 2,500 years after Khufu.
Earlier evidence exists in a few places, such as Egyptian names spelled in cuneiform letters of the New Kingdom (Ramesses II's name appears in Hittite records as Riamašeša), but it is patchy.
So vowels before Coptic are reconstructed with real uncertainty.
blocks.a: No: it shows only the late pronunciation.

blocks.html: Dialects add a further layer: the same word can have different vowels in Sahidic and Bohairic, as you will see in the next topic.
Applying Coptic vowels to Old Egyptian. Pronunciation changed over three thousand years. Use Coptic as evidence for late Egyptian sound, and treat earlier vowels as uncertain.

blocks.html: Egypt is a thousand kilometers long, and like any language spoken over a long country, Coptic had regional forms. Because Coptic writes vowels, the differences between them show clearly in writing.

Coptic had several dialects, chiefly Sahidic, the classical literary dialect of the south (Upper Egypt), and Bohairic, the dialect of the northwest Delta. Bohairic became the language of the Coptic Church's worship, and it is still used in Coptic services today.

Dialects follow geography. Sahidic flourished as a literary language from about the 4th to the 9th century AD, when the great monasteries of Upper Egypt were writing and copying books. Bohairic, spoken in the Delta near Alexandria and the important monasteries of Wadi al-Natrun, rose later; by the 11th century it had replaced Sahidic in the liturgy.

blocks.title: Why did Coptic fade?
blocks.q: After the Arab conquest of AD 641, how did Coptic lose its place as Egypt's everyday language?
steps: Arabic became the language of government around AD 700, and slowly the language of daily life.
Coptic was probably the majority language until somewhere between the 10th and 12th centuries, and survived as a spoken minority language until at least the 17th century.
It never died completely: it lived on in the Church's worship.
blocks.a: Slowly, over centuries, as Arabic spread; it survives in the Church.

blocks.title: Which dialect?
blocks.q: A Coptic text uses the letter ϧ. Which dialect is it most likely in?
steps: ϧ (khai) is one of the letters from Demotic.
Sahidic uses six such letters; Bohairic adds ϧ.
So the text is most likely Bohairic.
blocks.a: Bohairic.

blocks.html: Thinking Coptic died out completely. It survives in the worship of the Coptic Church, where Bohairic is read and sung, and since the 20th century there have been efforts to teach it more widely.

Writers like to say hieroglyphs ended with Cleopatra. In fact priests kept carving them for more than four centuries after her death in 30 BC, long after Coptic had begun. The very last known inscription is at Philae, the island temple of Isis near Aswan.

The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at Philae on 24 August AD 394, beside a figure of the Nubian god Mandulis, by a priest named Nesmeterakhem (also written Esmet-Akhom). A Demotic text beside it gives the date: the birthday of Osiris, in year 110 of the era of Diocletian.

Philae lay at Egypt's southern frontier, and its cult of Isis was honored by peoples from Nubia as well as Egypt. That helped it outlast the temples of the north, which closed under Christian emperors, especially after Theodosius I's laws against the old cults in 391–392. Philae's temple stayed open until about AD 535–537, when Justinian had it closed. Its last priests could still write the old scripts, but there was no one to teach them to.

blocks.title: No year zero
blocks.q: How many years passed between Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BC and the last hieroglyphic inscription in AD 394?
steps: Our calendar has no year 0: 1 BC is followed directly by AD 1.
From 30 BC to AD 1 is 30 years; from AD 1 to AD 394 is 393 years.
Total: 30 + 393 = 423 years. (The rule: BC years + AD years − 1.)
blocks.a: 423 years.

blocks.title: What the inscription says
blocks.q: The hieroglyphic text is a short dedication: before Mandulis, son of Horus, by Nesmeterakhem, "for all time and eternity". Why does such a small text matter so much?
steps: Its date is fixed exactly by the Demotic beside it.
No later hieroglyphic inscription is known, so it marks the end of more than 3,500 years of the script.
It shows the last generation of priests still working in the old way, in a Christian empire.
blocks.a: It is the last dated use of a script used for over 3,500 years.

blocks.html: The inscription is carved on the gateway of Hadrian, which led toward the Abaton, the sacred place on the neighboring island where Osiris was said to rest. Today the whole temple, gate and graffito included, stands on Agilkia, where it was moved during the Nubian campaign.
Dating the end of hieroglyphs to Cleopatra. They were carved for more than four centuries after her, until AD 394. Check by the gap: 423 years.
The last hieroglyphs were carved at Philae in AD 394. Demotic, the everyday script, lasted longer. Its last dated text is also at Philae.

The last dated Demotic inscription is a short graffito on the roof of the temple of Isis at Philae, dated to December AD 452: about sixty years after the last hieroglyphs. After that, Egyptian was written only in Coptic.

Demotic was more widely known than hieroglyphs: it was the script of documents, used by many more scribes. But by the 5th century its uses had shrunk to a few religious texts, mummy labels and graffiti, mostly written by priests and pilgrims. Philae, the last open temple, was where its last writers worked. Coptic, easier to learn, had taken over the rest.

blocks.html: Many of the last Demotic texts at Philae are short graffiti scratched by priests and visitors on the temple walls and roof: a name, a prayer, a date. They are small, but they are firm evidence that a few people, almost all of them connected with the temple, could still write the old script in the middle of the 5th century. Less than a century later, when Justinian closed the temple, the old Egyptian scripts were gone, and Coptic was the only way left to write the language.

blocks.title: Which ended first?
blocks.q: Did hieroglyphs or Demotic end first, and by how many years?
steps: Hieroglyphs: AD 394. Demotic: AD 452.
So hieroglyphs ended first; Demotic lasted about sixty years longer.
blocks.a: Hieroglyphs, by 58 years.

blocks.title: Across the era line
blocks.q: The first Demotic texts date from about 650 BC. For how many years was Demotic in use, up to AD 452?
steps: There is no year 0, so the span is 650 + 452 − 1.
About 1,100 years.
blocks.a: About 1,100 years.

blocks.html: Thinking hieroglyphs outlasted Demotic. Demotic lasted about sixty years longer. The formal script ended first because it was tied to the temples and their few trained carvers.

South of Egypt lay the kingdom of Kush, which you met in Egypt and Nubia. Its kings ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty and long afterward ruled from Napata and then Meroë. At first they wrote in Egyptian. From around the 3rd or 2nd century BC, while Egypt was writing in Demotic, they began to write their own language in a script of their own: Meroitic.

Meroitic has two forms: a monumental hieroglyphic form, with signs borrowed from Egyptian hieroglyphs, and a cursive form, derived from Demotic. Each has 23 signs. Francis Llewellyn Griffith worked out their sound values in 1909, so Meroitic can be read aloud, but much of the language is still not understood.

Reading a script and understanding a language are different problems. Griffith could find the sounds because Meroitic texts spell the names of kings, queens and gods that are known from Egyptian sources. But there is no long bilingual text, like the Rosetta Stone, and the Meroitic language has no well-known living relative, so most words cannot be translated. A few are known, such as qore "king" and kandake, the title of a ruling queen, which the Greeks and Romans heard as "Candace".

blocks.html: Meroitic is an alphasyllabary: a consonant sign is read with the vowel a unless a vowel sign follows. Words are separated by a mark of two or three dots. The language's family is debated: Claude Rilly and others argue that it belongs with the Eastern Sudanic languages, which include Nubian, while some scholars have proposed other links.

blocks.title: Reading without understanding
blocks.q: A Meroitic inscription can be sounded out completely. Why can't scholars translate it?
steps: Sound values come from names known in Egyptian sources.
Meanings need a bilingual text, or a well-understood related language, to compare with. Meroitic has neither in full.
So scholars can say the words but know the meaning of only some of them.
blocks.a: Sounds are known; most meanings are not.

blocks.title: Reading a sign
blocks.q: In Meroitic, a consonant sign alone carries the vowel a. How is the consonant k read alone, and how when followed by the vowel sign i?
steps: Alone, a consonant has the built-in vowel a: ka.
A following vowel sign replaces it: ki.
blocks.a: ka alone; ki with i.

blocks.html: Thinking being able to read a script means understanding it. Meroitic can be sounded out, but its meaning is only partly known.
